Tweedieverse

Nalin Arora, Ziyu Liu, Ali Rahnavard,Himel Mallick

21 November 2026

Source: vignettes/Tweedieverse.Rmd
Tweedieverse.Rmd

Overview

Tweedieverse provides a unified differential analysis workflow for omics measurements whose empirical variance structure is well represented by the Tweedie family. The framework is intended for heterogeneous high-throughput data, including microbiome abundances, single-cell RNA-seq measurements, bulk RNA-seq summaries, metabolite intensities, and other continuous or count-like assays.

The package uses Bioconductor containers as the primary interface. A single omics assay is represented as a SummarizedExperiment, TreeSummarizedExperiment, or SingleCellExperiment, and matched multi-omics assays are represented as a MultiAssayExperiment. This keeps feature assays, sample metadata, and experiment-level annotations together and makes the workflow compatible with the broader Bioconductor ecosystem.

This vignette demonstrates six Bioconductor-oriented workflows:

  • microbiome relative abundances stored in a TreeSummarizedExperiment,
  • single-cell RNA-seq UMI counts stored in a SingleCellExperiment,
  • single-cell RNA-seq non-UMI/read counts stored in a SingleCellExperiment,
  • pseudobulk RNA-seq counts generated with muscat::aggregateData(),
  • bulk RNA-seq counts from the Bioconductor airway dataset stored in a SummarizedExperiment,
  • matched microbiome and metabolomics assays stored in a MultiAssayExperiment.

Motivation

In omics data, biological processes or technical factors may induce distinct statistical properties (such as overdispersion and zero-inflation) across experimental platforms (or library preparation protocols). Most published differential analysis methods are omics-specific and assume a single probabilistic model for all features. DESeq2 and edgeR use the negative binomial distribution for sequencing counts. MAST uses a two-part hurdle model for single-cell expression. MaAsLin2 supports several microbiome association models, including linear and compound Poisson models, while MaAsLin3 models prevalence and abundance separately. limma fits linear models to expression data, including transformed RNA-seq measurements.

These choices ignore the fact that data distributions are feature-specific and vary considerably both within and between platforms or technologies. A typical multi-omics study therefore runs a different tool for each assay, each with its own assumptions, preprocessing, and output format, and the resulting effect sizes and significance calls are difficult to compare.

Tweedieverse provides a single home for differential analysis across omics data types. It is built on Tweedie generalized linear models, whose flexibility enables feature-specific modeling of omics data by adjusting a single configuration parameter per feature: the Tweedie index p, which spans the Gaussian, Poisson, compound Poisson-gamma, gamma, and inverse Gaussian distributions. Tweedieverse estimates p separately for each feature, so every feature is modeled with a mean-variance relationship learned from its own data. This yields a unified framework that adapts to biological and technological variability in multi-omics profiles. Model adequacy and study design determine the validity and power of the resulting tests; these examples demonstrate the workflow rather than benchmark comparative performance.

With Tweedieverse, users can:

  • run differential analysis on microbiome, single-cell, pseudobulk, bulk RNA-seq, and metabolomics data with one function, Tweedieverse();
  • pass data directly as a SummarizedExperiment, SingleCellExperiment, TreeSummarizedExperiment, or MultiAssayExperiment, with sample metadata and feature annotations kept intact;
  • compare results across assays on a common scale, since every assay is analyzed with the same model family, testing procedure, and output format.

The sections below walk through each of these workflows.

Relationship to existing tools

Bioconductor provides established differential-analysis workflows: DESeq2 and edgeR use negative-binomial models for sequencing counts; limma uses linear models with empirical Bayes inference, including precision-weighted RNA-seq analysis with voom. MAST uses a two-part hurdle model for single-cell detection and positive expression. MaAsLin2 offers multivariable meta-omic association analysis with several model choices, including compound Poisson models, while MaAsLin3 combines prevalence and abundance analyses.

Tweedie modeling is also available through general-purpose CRAN tools. cplm fits compound Poisson regression models, and glmmTMB supports Tweedie generalized linear mixed models. statmod supplies Tweedie GLM families, while tweedie provides distribution and likelihood calculations. Tweedieverse uses cplm, glmmTMB, and statmod as modeling engines.

Tweedieverse adds a common omics workflow around these engines: direct Bioconductor-container input, sample alignment, feature filtering, domain-specific size-factor offsets, feature-wise fitting, optional prevalence tests, multiple-testing correction, and consistently structured association tables. It supports both fixed and estimated variance powers and analyzes MultiAssayExperiment layers through the same interface. Each layer is fitted independently; effect sizes retain their assay- and link-specific interpretation.

Installation

After Bioconductor acceptance, the release version can be installed with:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}

BiocManager::install("Tweedieverse")

The development version can be installed from GitHub:

if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("remotes")
}

remotes::install_github("himelmallick/Tweedieverse")
library(Tweedieverse)
library(SummarizedExperiment)

Loading Packaged Example Data

The example containers used in this vignette are distributed with the package under inst/extdata. This allows the vignette to run during Bioconductor checks without network access.

The microbiome and UMI examples are compact subsets of the real HMP2 and PBMC3k datasets used in the original TweedieLabs tutorials. The non-UMI example uses CC BY 4.0 Tabula Muris Smart-seq2 brain data. The Franzosa multi-omics example comes from the HuMMANet v1 archive. The preparation code, source details, and per-object licences are included in scripts/rebuild_example_data.R, scripts/README.md, and extdata/DATA_LICENSES.md inside the installed package.

microbiome_tse <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "microbiome_tse.rds",
    package = "Tweedieverse"
))
umi_sce <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "umi_sce.rds",
    package = "Tweedieverse"
))
nonumi_sce <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "nonumi_sce.rds",
    package = "Tweedieverse"
))
franzosa_example_mae <- readRDS(system.file(
    "extdata", "franzosa_example_mae.rds",
    package = "Tweedieverse"
))

Microbiome Relative Abundance Example

For microbiome data, Tweedieverse() accepts a TreeSummarizedExperiment. The assay contains taxa/features in rows and samples in columns; colData contains sample metadata.

This subset contains the 20 most variable taxa across 48 baseline HMP2 samples, with 16 samples each from the nonIBD, CD, and UC groups. The source tables are distributed with MaAsLin2. Baseline selection and metadata preparation follow the original microbiome tutorial .

The example table contains relative abundances, so this analysis disables additional offset normalization by setting normalization = "NONE". For raw microbiome counts, omit that argument to use the microbiome default TSS size-factor offset.

microbiome_tse
#> class: TreeSummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 20 48 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(20): Prevotella copri Bacteroides vulgatus ... Veillonella
#>   unclassified Ruminococcus torques
#> rowData names(0):
#> colnames(48): CSM67UH7 CSM6J2H9_P ... MSM5LLIQ_P MSM79HBZ
#> colData names(11): site age ... dysbiosisCD collection
#> reducedDimNames(0):
#> mainExpName: NULL
#> altExpNames(0):
#> rowLinks: NULL
#> rowTree: NULL
#> colLinks: NULL
#> colTree: NULL

microbiome_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = microbiome_tse,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "microbiome",
    normalization = "NONE",
    fixed_effects = c("diagnosis", "antibiotics", "age"),
    reference = "diagnosis,nonIBD",
    return_all = TRUE,
    tweedie_p = NULL,
    median_comparison = FALSE
)

Reading the result table

Each row describes one feature–covariate coefficient. Factor variables can produce several rows per feature, one per non-reference level. These examples use median_comparison = FALSE and the default log link.

  • feature , metadata , value : Feature identifier, tested covariate, and factor level or continuous predictor name. Factor effects are relative to the reference level.
  • coef , stderr : Estimated coefficient and its standard error on the link scale. With a log link, exp(coef) is the fitted mean ratio at equal offsets. Continuous covariates are standardized by default, so their coefficients describe a one-standard-deviation increase unless standardize = FALSE .
  • pval , qval : Unadjusted test p-value and multiple-testing adjusted p-value (Benjamini–Hochberg by default across the reported coefficient tests within an assay).
  • base.model , tweedie.index : Model engine/family label and estimated or fixed variance power.
  • N , N.not.zero , percent.zero : Aligned sample count, number with positive measurements, and rounded percentage of observed measurements equal to zero. Missing model covariates can reduce a particular fit’s effective sample count.

return_all = TRUE keeps the full result table in memory. The default returns only rows with qval <= max_significance (default 0.05). An empty default table means no returned associations meet that cutoff, rather than no models were attempted. Failed fits produce feature-named warnings and are absent from the result table; inspect those warnings before interpreting the results. The number of hypotheses here covers only the selected features; these q-values are not results from testing the entire source dataset.

diagnosis_results <- subset(microbiome_fit, metadata == "diagnosis")
diagnosis_results$mean_ratio <- exp(diagnosis_results$coef)
head(diagnosis_results[, c(
    "feature", "value", "coef", "mean_ratio", "pval", "qval"
)], 2)
#>                    feature value      coef  mean_ratio         pval       qval
#> 1      Clostridium bolteae    CD  3.133765 22.96026215 0.0004870498 0.03506759
#> 2 Bacteroides massiliensis    CD -3.849450  0.02129144 0.0013718752 0.04938751

The first displayed diagnosis association is Clostridium bolteae in CD relative to nonIBD: its coefficient is 3.13 and its adjusted p-value is 0.0351. The second is Bacteroides massiliensis, with coefficient -3.85 and adjusted p-value 0.0494. A positive coefficient indicates higher fitted relative abundance and a negative coefficient lower fitted relative abundance, adjusting for age and antibiotic use. These are conditional associations in this subset, not evidence of causality.

Visualizing associations

For an exploratory overview, the heatmap below includes associations meeting qval <= 0.25, an explicitly relaxed 25% FDR threshold. It shows up to five features and all retained contrasts for those features. The package heatmap uses signed -log(qval), clipped to [-20, 20]: red denotes positive abundance coefficients and blue negative coefficients. Larger magnitudes indicate stronger evidence. Empty feature–contrast combinations are displayed as zero; they do not establish absence of an effect. The plot’s significance label refers to the chosen 0.25 cutoff.

heatmap_results <- subset(microbiome_fit, !is.na(qval) & qval <= 0.25)
Tweedieverse_heatmap(
    output_results = heatmap_results,
    cell_value = "qval",
    first_n = 5,
    title = "HMP2 associations (q <= 0.25)",
    data_label = "Taxon",
    metadata_label = "Covariate / contrast"
)

Single-Cell RNA-seq UMI Count Example

For single-cell RNA-seq data, Tweedieverse() accepts a SingleCellExperiment. The UMI example uses integer molecule counts.

This subset contains 20 genes and 60 PBMC3k cells, with 30 CD4 and 30 CD8 cells. Cell labels and raw UMI counts come from the processed object used in the original UMI tutorial . Genes are selected by count variance across the retained cells.

UMI counts are count-like. Here we pin the variance power to p = 1, the Poisson variance case, and use the single-cell domain. The library sizes in colData were calculated using all source genes before selecting the 20 genes. Passing scale_factor = "library_size" uses those full-library sizes as offsets.

umi_sce
#> class: SingleCellExperiment 
#> dim: 20 60 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(20): MALAT1 TMSB4X ... RPS27A RPL10A
#> rowData names(0):
#> colnames(60): AAACGCTGACCAGT AAACGCTGGTTCTT ... AACCTACTGTGTTG
#>   AACCTTACGAGACG
#> colData names(8): orig.ident nCount_RNA ... CellType library_size
#> reducedDimNames(0):
#> mainExpName: NULL
#> altExpNames(0):

umi_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = umi_sce,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "single_cell",
    scale_factor = "library_size",
    fixed_effects = "CellType",
    reference = "CellType,CD8",
    tweedie_p = 1,
    median_comparison = FALSE
)

The CellType rows compare CD4 with the CD8 reference group. For example, RPS6 has coefficient 0.4 and q-value 0.00192. At equal library size, its fitted CD4/CD8 mean ratio is 1.49. This is a cell-type illustration from one donor. Cells are not independent biological replicates for population-level treatment inference; use replicated samples and an appropriate design for that question.

Single-Cell RNA-seq Non-UMI / Read Count Example

The non-UMI example uses read-count-like measurements. These can have a more flexible mean-variance relationship than UMI counts, so we leave tweedie_p = NULL and let Tweedieverse estimate the index after filtering.

The source is the original Tabula Muris Smart-seq2 FACS dataset, distributed under CC BY 4.0 in Figshare version 8. This example retains 20 genes and 60 cells from mouse 3_10_M, balanced between astrocytes and oligodendrocytes. The SCRAN factors in colData were computed on all source genes for these cells before selecting the 20 most variable genes. The source counts are unchanged. This is a cell-type illustration within one mouse; it does not establish population-level differential expression across biological replicates. See the original study.

nonumi_sce
#> class: SingleCellExperiment 
#> dim: 20 60 
#> metadata(8): dataset source_doi ... source_md5 processing
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(20): Rn45s Plp1 ... Gsn Mfge8
#> rowData names(0):

Here the contrast is oligodendrocytes relative to astrocytes. The first returned gene, Trf, has coefficient 9.97, q-value 4^{-27}, and fitted variance power 1.693. The coefficient’s sign describes the direction after accounting for the precomputed SCRAN factor. The fitted index describes the variance model; it is not an effect size or significance measure.

Pseudobulk Single-Cell RNA-seq Example

Pseudobulk analysis aggregates single-cell counts to sample-level counts before modeling. This is useful when the biological replicate, rather than the cell, is the experimental unit. The muscat package provides a Bioconductor-native workflow for this aggregation. Its aggregateData() function summarizes a SingleCellExperiment by variables in colData, commonly cluster_id and sample_id.

This example follows the workflow used by the muscat vignette: multi-subject single-cell data are first represented as a prepared SingleCellExperiment, cells are aggregated into cluster-by-sample pseudobulk counts, and the resulting sample-level count matrix is analyzed with Tweedieverse(). The package-provided example_sce object contains the required cluster_id, sample_id, and group_id fields and is a lightweight version of the Kang et al. interferon stimulation example used throughout muscat.

data("example_sce", package = "muscat")

pseudobulk_input <- example_sce[seq_len(100), ]

pseudobulk_sce <- muscat::aggregateData(
    pseudobulk_input,
    assay = "counts",
    fun = "sum",
    by = c("cluster_id", "sample_id"),
    verbose = FALSE
)

SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(pseudobulk_sce)
#> [1] "B cells"           "CD14+ Monocytes"   "CD4 T cells"      
#> [4] "CD8 T cells"       "FCGR3A+ Monocytes"

pseudobulk_assay <- "CD4 T cells"
pseudobulk_counts <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(
    pseudobulk_sce,
    pseudobulk_assay
)
top_pseudobulk_genes <- order(
    rowSums(pseudobulk_counts),
    decreasing = TRUE
)[seq_len(20)]

pseudobulk_metadata <- unique(as.data.frame(
    SummarizedExperiment::colData(pseudobulk_input)[, c("sample_id",
        "group_id")]
))
rownames(pseudobulk_metadata) <- pseudobulk_metadata$sample_id
pseudobulk_metadata <- pseudobulk_metadata[
    colnames(pseudobulk_counts), ,
    drop = FALSE
]
pseudobulk_metadata$condition <- pseudobulk_metadata$group_id

pseudobulk_se <- SummarizedExperiment::SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = pseudobulk_counts[top_pseudobulk_genes, , drop =
        FALSE]),
    colData = pseudobulk_metadata
)

pseudobulk_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = pseudobulk_se,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "bulk_rnaseq",
    fixed_effects = c("condition"),
    reference = "condition,ctrl",
    tweedie_p = 1,
    median_comparison = FALSE,
    max_significance = 1
)

The condition coefficient compares stimulated samples with control samples within CD4 T cells. For IFI6, the coefficient is 3.88 and q-value is 0.1. The rows represent sample-level pseudobulks rather than individual cells, so N counts pseudobulk samples. max_significance = 1 displays all available tests, including weak evidence; it does not declare them all significant. This compact example omits donor blocking; a paired stimulation study should include donor in the model.

Bulk RNA-seq Count Example

For bulk RNA-seq data, Tweedieverse() accepts a SummarizedExperiment. This example uses the Bioconductor airway dataset, which contains RNA-seq read counts from airway smooth muscle cells treated with dexamethasone.

The full airway object contains tens of thousands of genes. To keep the vignette fast, the example keeps a small set of high-count genes while preserving the original airway sample metadata. Bulk RNA-seq uses TMM as the default normalization strategy in Tweedieverse; this computes library-size factors for the model offset without modifying the count assay.

Set run_presence_absence_model = TRUE to include a test for whether the feature is detected. By default, the prevalence fit requires at least three samples with nonzero counts and three with zero counts for each gene. Use min_presence_absence_count to change both minimums. In bulk and pseudobulk data, genes with only one or two zeros can still enter the abundance analysis. For retained genes below either minimum, pval_presence is NA and pval_abundance becomes the joint pval. When the two reported p-values are exactly 0 and 1, the joint pval is 0. Tweedieverse applies the selected multiple-testing correction to the joint p-values to compute qval.

Use return_all = TRUE to retrieve the full association table with output = NULL, including associations above max_significance. The default returns associations passing the threshold. Missing q-values after median comparison are retained in the full table and excluded from significant results.

data("airway", package = "airway")

airway_counts <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(airway, "counts")
top_airway_genes <- order(rowSums(airway_counts), decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(
    20)]

bulk_rnaseq_se <- SummarizedExperiment::SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = airway_counts[top_airway_genes, , drop = FALSE]),
    colData = SummarizedExperiment::colData(airway)
)

bulk_rnaseq_se
#> class: SummarizedExperiment 
#> dim: 20 8 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(20): ENSG00000115414 ENSG00000011465 ... ENSG00000137801
#>   ENSG00000142173
#> rowData names(0):
#> colnames(8): SRR1039508 SRR1039509 ... SRR1039520 SRR1039521
#> colData names(9): SampleName cell ... Sample BioSample

bulk_rnaseq_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = bulk_rnaseq_se,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "counts",
    domain = "bulk_rnaseq",
    fixed_effects = c("dex"),
    reference = "dex,untrt",
    tweedie_p = 1,
    median_comparison = FALSE,
    run_presence_absence_model = TRUE,
    max_significance = 0.05,
    return_all = TRUE
)

The dex contrast compares dexamethasone-treated with untreated samples. For ENSG00000108821, coef_abundance is -0.83 and the joint q-value is 0.00165. A positive abundance coefficient indicates higher offset-adjusted mean counts in treated samples.

With the presence model enabled, coef and stderr retain abundance-model meaning; the joint CCT p-value is not a test of a combined effect size. coef_presence is a logistic-model log-odds coefficient, while pval_abundance/qval_abundance and pval_presence/qval_presence describe component tests. Inspect pval_presence to see which genes lacked enough zeros or detections to fit the prevalence model. For those genes, the joint p-value falls back to the abundance p-value. return_all = TRUE includes rows above 0.05; use subset(bulk_rnaseq_fit, !is.na(qval) & qval <= 0.05) for discovery selection. The full airway experiment is paired by cell line; include cell alongside dex when analyzing that study design.

Multi-omics Container

For multi-omics data, Tweedieverse() accepts a MultiAssayExperiment. The packaged Franzosa et al. example is stored as an individual .rds file in inst/extdata. It contains matched microbiome species abundances and metabolite profiles. Each omics layer is analyzed independently, and per-omics parameters can be supplied as named vectors or lists.

franzosa_example_mae
#> A MultiAssayExperiment object of 2 listed
#>  experiments with user-defined names and respective classes.
#>  Containing an ExperimentList class object of length 2:
#>  [1] taxaAbundanceProfile: SummarizedExperiment with 4 rows and 16 columns
#>  [2] harmonizedMetaboliteProfile: SummarizedExperiment with 4 rows and 16 columns
#> Functionality:
#>  experiments() - obtain the ExperimentList instance
#>  colData() - the primary/phenotype DataFrame
#>  sampleMap() - the sample coordination DataFrame
#>  `$`, `[`, `[[` - extract colData columns, subset, or experiment
#>  *Format() - convert into a long or wide DataFrame
#>  assays() - convert ExperimentList to a SimpleList of matrices
#>  exportClass() - save data to flat files

multi_fit <- Tweedieverse(
    input_features = franzosa_example_mae,
    output = NULL,
    assay_name = "abundance",
    domain = c(
        taxaAbundanceProfile = "microbiome",
        harmonizedMetaboliteProfile = "custom"
    ),
    normalization = c(
        taxaAbundanceProfile = "NONE",
        harmonizedMetaboliteProfile = "MEDIAN"
    ),
    fixed_effects = c("diseaseCat_clean", "Age"),
    tweedie_p = list(
        taxaAbundanceProfile = NULL,
        harmonizedMetaboliteProfile = NULL
    ),
    median_comparison = FALSE,
    max_significance = 1
)

Each list element is a separate association table, and its omics column identifies the layer. diseaseCat_clean rows compare the named value with the reference disease category; Age rows describe a one-standard-deviation increase because continuous predictors are standardized by default. Within either layer, a positive log-link coefficient means a higher fitted mean, conditional on the other covariate and offset. Taxon abundances and metabolite intensities have different measurement scales, so coefficients should be interpreted within layers. q-values are adjusted separately per layer, not across the entire multi-omics list. As above, max_significance = 1 displays tests without requiring a discovery threshold.

Median comparison uses Monte Carlo simulations when median_comparison = TRUE. Set median_comparison_seed = 123 to reproduce those simulations. The seed is scoped with withr, restoring the preceding random-number state after the median-comparison calculation. When the seed is NULL, results can vary between runs.
